startup.name: herdr
startup.description:
Developers don't run one coding agent anymore. They run fleets of them — for hours, sometimes days — across laptops, servers, and sandboxes. Keeping track of that work is the new bottleneck: which agent is blocked, which one finished, which terminal is it in, and why did everything die when the laptop closed.

Herdr is the open-source home for that work. A background server owns the agents' terminal sessions on each machine, so the work survives disconnects, closed lids, and dropped SSH. Herdr detects each agent and turns the chaos into an attention queue — working, blocked, done, across every project — so you look only when an agent needs you. Every client is just a view: the bundled terminal UI, SSH from another machine, your phone. Close one, open another; the work never stops.

Software can drive it too: a CLI, a socket API, and a plugin marketplace that passed 500 community plugins

yc_acceptance.basis: Starting rate is about 1 percent with a 0.6 to 2 percent band. The company is already accepted, so this is a note only. A solo founder lowers odds slightly, but 25k GitHub stars, 340k downloads and a large plugin ecosystem are far stronger traction than most applicants show, which lifts the odds several times.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: YC would most plausibly say no because the founder is solo and the product is free open source with no revenue. Reviewers would worry that terminal tooling for coding agents is a feature that Anthropic, OpenAI or editors will ship, and that an Apache licensed runtime has no clear way to make money.

ladder.why_it_fails: Series B fails if the project remains a developer convenience and not a revenue engine. Open source companies need a paid tier with strong conversion, and rivals can fork under the Apache license. continue reached only a 3M seed before being acquired by Cursor. Reaching this step also takes time, and the milestone can slip by a year or more before investors accept the evidence, so the odds here already account for timing risk, thin traction data and the small sample behind the cohort anchors.

killers.risk: Platform vendors build session management into their agent clients
killers.evidence: Anthropic, OpenAI and editors already ship cloud and background agents and could add attention queues.
killers.mitigation: Stay agent neutral and own the cross machine runtime and plugin ecosystem.

killers.risk: No monetization for a free Apache licensed runtime
killers.evidence: cmux has strong adoption but no round beyond YC, and terminal tools rarely charge.
killers.mitigation: Hosted sync, team features and enterprise control plane.

killers.risk: Solo founder cannot scale support and security trust
killers.evidence: The team is one person with a background project in Turkey, and a runtime that owns sessions must be reliable.
killers.mitigation: Hire early from the open source community.

killers.risk: Hype fades as agents shift to cloud sandboxes
killers.evidence: Many coding agents are moving to hosted environments, reducing local terminal usage.
killers.mitigation: Support remote and sandbox machines as first class.

technical_complexity.rationale: A persistent background server that owns terminal sessions, detects agent states across many tools and syncs across machines is a manageable engineering task for one strong developer. The hard parts are reliable agent detection as tools change and security of remote access, which grow with scale.

takeover_risk.rationale: Agent vendors could add attention queues and persistence to their own clients in months. The open license and plugin ecosystem make it a community standard if neutral, but a platform feature could remove demand.

evidence.claim: Several tools already compete to replace tmux for agent fleets, showing developer demand for agent aware session management.
tmux has no concept of agent state, which is the stated gap.

actions: Launch hosted sync and team tier

pros.evidence: 25k stars and 340k downloads reported four months after launch, with 500 community plugins.
Fleets of coding agents need persistence and attention routing, which tmux does not provide.

narrative.headline: An open source agent runtime with unusual traction and a probable seed, but monetization and platform risk limit later rounds.
narrative.general_summary: Herdr is a free Apache licensed runtime that keeps coding agent terminals alive and routes attention across machines. Its reported traction is much higher than typical YC applicants and a seed above the YC deal looks likely. The main risks are solo founder, no revenue, and agent vendors shipping similar features. Open source developer tool cohorts reach Series A at about 39 percent of seed companies, and the comps cmux, continue and fig show adoption without large rounds. The estimates rest on cohort base rates, a handful of real analogs and market searches limited to information available at the batch start, so they carry wide uncertainty and should be read as ranges, not points.

assumptions: Blind test: only the batch input file was used for the company.
A seed here means a round above the YC deal of about 500K within about 12 months of the batch start.
A market search result named this company directly; it was ignored (LEAK-WEB).
Traction figures come from the company description and are unverified.
